newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Slack imports dent Australia investment hopes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Slack imports dent Australia investment hopes.

text.p: Australian merchandise imports figures released on Tuesday provided further evidence of a subdued economy and suggested policy makers' upbeat forecasts for business investment might be a little too optimistic.
Imports rose 1.3 percent overall which was much in line with market estimates, but imports of capital goods such as machinery slid 7.1 percent to be 3.6 percent down on the year.
"There is little sign of life in the economy at present," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank. "The imports data confirm the lack of confidence to spend or invest."

The fall in capital imports for October all but wiped out gains seen the previous two months and meant imports so far in 1996/97 fiscal year were running 2.8 percent down on the same period in 1995/96.

That mattered for assessments of business investment since a big chunk of spending on plant and equipment went on imports and the government was looking for an impressive 14 percent rise in investment in the 1996/97 year.
"The setback in October is a clear signal the budget time forecast for capital expenditure is too high," said Matthew Drennan, an economist at Axiom Funds Management.
That would also be of concern to the Reserve Bank which had highlighted business investment as the "linchpin of forecast growth" in its last quarterly review of the economy.

Analysts reckoned that if the impression of a softening in investment intentions was confirmed by third quarter capital expenditure data, due next week, then the case for another easing in monetary policy would be significantly strengthened.
Indeed, Kunnen at Colonial thought the case already was airtight.
"Further monteary stimulus will be required. It is now a question of when official rates are cut," he said.

Other analysts cautioned that the government's investment forecasts could not be downgraded just yet since much of the growth expected was in buildings and structures, which are far less import sensitive.
For the rest of the economy, the imports data painted a mixed picture with pockets of both strength and weakness.
Imports of consumption goods fell 1.2 percent in seasonally adjusted terms on top of a 4.7 percent fall in September, but were still 8.8 percent higher on the year.
The seasonal adjustment is quite significant in October as in original terms consumption goods imports rose 16 percent.
Imports of intermediate and other goods, a catch-all for such things as machinery parts, plastics and paper, rose 6.9 percent on the month, largely due to a huge 116 percent jump in fuel imports.
From the balance of payments perspective, the data suggested October would see a similar deficit to September's surprisingly high A$1.69 billion, if not a little higher.

"They imply a deficit of around A$1.75 billion," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia. "The mild deterioration issues warning of potential current account pressure in 1997." -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
